title: 265. Functions, Graphs & Transformations: Rational Function Vertical Asymptotes
description: A comprehensive mathematics curriculum progressing from foundational numeracy and core mathematical concepts to algebra, geometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, optimization, mathematical foundations of AI, advanced pure mathematics, and emerging research methods.

questions.concept: Vertical Asymptote of a Simple Rational Function
questions.learningObjective: Determine the vertical asymptote of a rational function with a linear denominator.
questions.question: What is the vertical asymptote of the graph of \(f(x)=\frac{1}{x-3}\)?
questions.explanation: A vertical asymptote occurs where the denominator is zero and the numerator is not zero. Set \(x-3=0\), giving \(x=3\). The numerator is \(1\), which is not zero at \(x=3\). Therefore the vertical asymptote is \(x=3\), so option A is correct.
questions.hint: Find the value of \(x\) that makes the denominator zero.

questions.concept: Vertical Asymptote of a Simple Rational Function
questions.learningObjective: Determine the vertical asymptote of a rational function with a linear denominator.
questions.question: What is the vertical asymptote of the graph of \(f(x)=\frac{1}{x+2}\)?
questions.explanation: Set the denominator equal to zero: \(x+2=0\), so \(x=-2\). The numerator \(1\) is not zero at \(x=-2\). Therefore the vertical asymptote is \(x=-2\), so option B is correct.
questions.hint: A vertical asymptote occurs where the denominator is zero and the numerator is not zero.

questions.concept: Vertical Asymptotes of a Rational Function with a Factored Denominator
questions.learningObjective: Determine all vertical asymptotes from a factored denominator.
questions.question: What are the vertical asymptotes of \(f(x)=\frac{x+1}{(x-2)(x+3)}\)?
questions.explanation: Set each denominator factor equal to zero: \(x-2=0\) gives \(x=2\), and \(x+3=0\) gives \(x=-3\). At both values, the numerator \(x+1\) is not zero. Therefore the vertical asymptotes are \(x=2\) and \(x=-3\), so option B is correct.
questions.hint: Set each factor in the denominator equal to zero and check the numerator.

questions.concept: Distinguishing a Hole from a Vertical Asymptote
questions.learningObjective: Identify the vertical asymptote after recognizing a common factor that creates a hole.
questions.question: What is the vertical asymptote of \(f(x)=\frac{x-1}{(x-1)(x+2)}\)?
questions.explanation: The factor \(x-1\) appears in both numerator and denominator, so \(x=1\) is a hole, not a vertical asymptote. After canceling, \(f(x)=\frac{1}{x+2}\) for \(x\ne 1\). The remaining denominator \(x+2\) is zero at \(x=-2\), and the numerator is not zero there. Therefore the vertical asymptote is \(x=-2\), so option A is correct.
questions.hint: Cancel common factors first; a canceled factor usually indicates a hole.

questions.concept: Rational Function with No Vertical Asymptote after Cancellation
questions.learningObjective: Determine that a rational function has no vertical asymptote when every denominator factor cancels with the numerator.
questions.question: Which statement is correct for \(f(x)=\frac{x^2-4}{x-2}\)?

options.label: A
options.text: The graph has a vertical asymptote at \(x=2\).

options.label: B
options.text: The graph has no vertical asymptote.

questions.explanation: Factor the numerator: \(x^2-4=(x-2)(x+2)\). Then \(f(x)=\frac{(x-2)(x+2)}{x-2}=x+2\) for \(x\ne 2\). The factor \(x-2\) cancels, so \(x=2\) is a hole, not a vertical asymptote. Therefore there is no vertical asymptote, so option B is correct.
questions.hint: After canceling common factors, check whether any denominator factor remains.

questions.concept: Distinguishing a Hole from a Vertical Asymptote
questions.learningObjective: Identify the vertical asymptote when one denominator factor cancels with the numerator.
questions.question: What is the vertical asymptote of \(f(x)=\frac{x+3}{x^2-9}\)?
questions.explanation: Factor the denominator: \(x^2-9=(x-3)(x+3)\). The factor \(x+3\) cancels with the numerator, so \(x=-3\) is a hole. After canceling, \(f(x)=\frac{1}{x-3}\) for \(x\ne -3\). The remaining denominator is zero at \(x=3\), so the vertical asymptote is \(x=3\). Therefore option A is correct.
questions.hint: Factor the denominator and cancel any common factor before finding the asymptote.

questions.concept: Rational Function with an Always-Positive Denominator
questions.learningObjective: Determine that a rational function has no vertical asymptote when the denominator is never zero.
questions.question: Which statement is correct for \(f(x)=\frac{2x}{x^2+1}\)?

options.label: A
options.text: The graph has no vertical asymptote.

options.label: B
options.text: The graph has a vertical asymptote at \(x=0\).

questions.explanation: The denominator is \(x^2+1\). For every real number \(x\), \(x^2\ge 0\), so \(x^2+1\ge 1>0\). The denominator is never zero. Therefore the graph has no vertical asymptote, so option A is correct.
questions.hint: Check whether the denominator can ever equal zero for real values of \(x\).

questions.concept: Vertical Asymptote after Canceling a Common Factor
questions.learningObjective: Determine the vertical asymptote after simplifying a rational function.
questions.question: What is the vertical asymptote of \(f(x)=\frac{x^2-1}{x^2-3x+2}\)?
questions.explanation: Factor numerator and denominator: \(x^2-1=(x-1)(x+1)\) and \(x^2-3x+2=(x-1)(x-2)\). Cancel \(x-1\), so \(f(x)=\frac{x+1}{x-2}\) for \(x\ne 1\). The canceled factor gives a hole at \(x=1\). The remaining denominator is zero at \(x=2\), so the only vertical asymptote is \(x=2\). Therefore option A is correct.
questions.hint: Factor both numerator and denominator, then cancel common factors before identifying vertical asymptotes.

questions.concept: Vertical Asymptote after Canceling a Common Factor
questions.learningObjective: Determine whether a canceled factor creates a hole or a vertical asymptote.
questions.question: Which statement is correct for \(f(x)=\frac{x^2+2x}{x^2-4}\)?
questions.explanation: Factor numerator and denominator: \(x^2+2x=x(x+2)\) and \(x^2-4=(x-2)(x+2)\). Cancel \(x+2\), so \(f(x)=\frac{x}{x-2}\) for \(x\ne -2\). The canceled factor gives a hole at \(x=-2\). The remaining denominator is zero at \(x=2\), so only \(x=2\) is a vertical asymptote. Therefore option B is correct.
questions.hint: A canceled factor produces a hole, not a vertical asymptote.

questions.concept: Vertical Asymptote after Full Factorization and Cancellation
questions.learningObjective: Determine the vertical asymptote of a rational function after simplifying by canceling a common factor.
questions.question: What is the vertical asymptote of \(f(x)=\frac{x^2-5x+6}{x^2-4x+3}\)?
questions.explanation: Factor numerator and denominator: \(x^2-5x+6=(x-2)(x-3)\) and \(x^2-4x+3=(x-1)(x-3)\). Cancel \(x-3\), so \(f(x)=\frac{x-2}{x-1}\) for \(x\ne 3\). The canceled factor gives a hole at \(x=3\). The remaining denominator is zero at \(x=1\), so the vertical asymptote is \(x=1\). Therefore option A is correct.
questions.hint: Factor completely, cancel common factors, and then set the remaining denominator equal to zero.
